newsitem.title: USA: Foster Wheeler appeals incinerator suit dismissal.
newsitem.headline: Foster Wheeler appeals incinerator suit dismissal.

text.p: Foster Wheeler Corp continued its legal battle against Illinois by appealing the dismissal of its lawsuit contesting the loss of an incinerator subsidy in the U.S. Appeals Court in Chicago.

Tom O'Brien, senior vice president and general counsel at the Clinton, N.J.-based company, said Tuesday that a notice of appeal was filed on Monday and that the company would file a brief in the case within the next couple of months.

The appeal came in the wake of a U.S. District Court judge's dismissal of Foster Wheeler's lawsuit on Nov 1. At that time, Judge James Zagel dismissed the case on the ground the 11th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution procludes lawsuits against states dealing with public funds.
In his ruling, Zagel also said that while the company's claims in the lawsuit may have merit, the case should be litigated in state court and not federal court.

On Nov 22, Robbins Resource Recovery Partners, the developer of a bond-financed incinerator in the Chicago suburb of Robbins, as well as the village of Robbins, filed a lawsuit against state officials in Cook County Circuit Court. Foster Wheeler is the general partner of the resource recovery partnership.
Foster Wheeler's original lawsuit was filed in federal court shortly after Gov. Jim Edgar in March signed into law a bill repealing a state law that provided a subsidy for incinerators.
That law had allowed waste-to-energy incinerators to sell electricity they produced to utilities at a higher rate subsidized by the state.
Both the federal and the state court lawsuits claimed the removal of the subsidy violated various constitutional provisions, including due process, impairment of contract and equal protection.
O'Brien said the company is also reviewing a plan to seek administrative relief from state agencies.
"We're trying to do everything we can to rectify the situation," he said.
Robbins sold $320 million of unrated, tax-exempt bonds for the incinerator in 1994.

As a result of the lost subsidy, the suburb completed a tender in October of nearly all the bonds for new bonds with lower interest rates, some extended maturities, additional credit support from Foster Wheeler, new convenants and different redemption provisions.
Two other lawsuits filed by incinerator developers are also pending against Illinois officials in state courts.
